metadata.title: PIRLS 2006 Assessment Framework and Specifications — 2nd Edition
metadata.venue: TIMSS & PIRLS International Study Center (Boston College) / IEA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This document is an assessment framework and specifications for PIRLS 2006 rather than an empirical analysis paper. It describes the assessment design (matrix sampling of test booklets, questionnaire instruments, and scaling via item response theory) but does not provide an analytic dataset or report any student-level estimation results. Therefore, it does not specify whether analysts should apply student/sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in statistical analyses. For PIRLS analyses using the eventual PIRLS 2006 database, analysts should follow IEA’s standard complex survey procedures for matrix-sampled assessments and use the provided sampling/replicate weights when producing population-representative estimates; however, this framework text itself does not name specific weight variables.

data.outcome_summary: PIRLS 2006 is designed to measure reading literacy for students in their fourth year of formal schooling, focusing on comprehension processes and reading purposes. The written assessment uses authentic literary and informational passages, with each passage accompanied by multiple-choice and constructed-response items; the assessment is organized into a matrix-sampling design with 10 blocks of 40 minutes distributed across 13 student booklets (including a color “Reader” booklet). Achievement reporting is planned on an overall reading literacy scale and separate scales for two purposes (literary experience; acquire and use information) and two comprehension processes (retrieval & straightforward inferences; interpreting, integrating & evaluating). Student and contextual questionnaires (students, parents/caregivers, teachers, principals, and a curriculum questionnaire) are included to support analyses of home and school factors. The document specifies scaling via item response theory and describes how items are linked across booklets, but it does not provide empirical model results, performance metrics, or a PV/missing-data handling procedure for an analysis sample.
